items.text: Trump wants South Korea in on Alaska LNG. Here’s why Seoul is cautious
items.article: South Korea remains cautious on Alaska LNG amid concerns over its high costs and commercial risks. South Korea is taking a cautious approach to the long-planned Alaska liquefied natural gas project, despite U.S. President Donald Trump touting it as part of Seoul's $200 billion investment package in the U.S. Trump said late Wednesday that the two countries had agreed to work on the $50 billion project, but South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pushed back, saying South Korea's participation would hinge on its financial viability and legal compliance. At the heart of the debate is the scale and cost of getting Alaska's vast natural gas resources to overseas buyers. The Alaska LNG project seeks to transport natural gas through an approximately 800-mile pipeline from Prudhoe Bay in Alaska's North Slope to an LNG facility in Nikiski in the south, according to the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation. The integrated project, which would have capacity to produce 20 million metric tons of LNG annually, is estimated to cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion, according to Go Katayama, principal insight analyst at Kpler. Shipping LNG from Nikiski to South Korea would take roughly seven to nine days, compared with around 20 to 30 days from the U.S. Gulf Coast, according to Seung Hoon Yoo, professor at the Department of Future Energy Convergence at Seoul National University of Science and Technology.

items.key: ai:how claims of 'masking' in adhd are impacting diagnosis
items.text: How claims of 'masking' in ADHD are impacting diagnosis
items.article: The idea that people can 'mask' symptoms of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder has contributed to the rise in diagnoses, but is it based on good evidence? ADHD is a medical condition that is currently under intense scrutiny. Numbers of those diagnosed are rising, waiting lists are lengthening – and the benefits bill is swelling. Along with similar rises in autism and mental ill health , the trend is causing such concern, it’s the subject of a government investigation, due to report shortly . One aspect of the rise in ADHD that gets less attention is “masking” – the idea that people cover up symptoms such as disorganisation, fidgeting and daydreaming to cope better with school or work. This may have contributed to a significant portion of the rise in ADHD diagnoses over the past decade, and possibly to the rise in autism too, say experts. But some doctors and researchers are sceptical about the entire premise of masking. “It’s an unfalsifiable concept,” said Professor Uta Frith, an Emeritus Professor of Cognitive Development at University College London. The government review into ADHD, autism and mental health conditions was ordered by Health Secretary Wes Streeting last year.

items.article: This week, LeT commander Mohammad Asif was killed in a gunfight in Yusmarg. Security agencies say the group operated across the Pir Panjal for nearly five years, carrying out attacks in Rajouri, Gulmarg and Pahalgam before its members were gradually tracked down. For nearly five years, Lashkar-e-Toiba (LeT) commander Mohammad Asif moved through the forests of the Pir Panjal and Kashmir Valley, part of a network behind a string of deadly attacks targeting civilians and security forces while evading capture. On Wednesday, Asif, also known as Hashim Moosa, was killed in a gunfight with security forces — the latest breakthrough in the hunt for the network, which was linked to attacks across the region, including the April 2025 Pahalgam attack that killed 26 people , including a local pony operator. According to officials, LeT commander Mohammad Asif, whom sources describe as highly trained and battle-hardened, had been acting alone after his associate Yasir was killed in a gunfight in Ashdar Gali in the upper reaches of Dodapathri tourist resort last month. Sources say Asif – as well as his two partners Yasir and Sulaiman – infiltrated the forests of Jammu in late 2021 and have been active since, with investigators saying they were responsible for several deadly terror attacks on the Rajouri-Poonch axis. Officials claim that it was this group that was involved in several gunfights in Bhatta Durian in Rajouri in October 2021, leading to the killings of as many as nine soldiers.

items.text: I’m a former flight attendant. Here are 9 things I wish passengers would stop doing on airplanes.
items.article: I saw far too many people go to the lavatory barefoot or blast music without headphones. I worked as a flight attendant on long-haul international routes for nearly a decade — and I got an unfiltered, front-row seat to some of the worst passenger etiquette in commercial air travel. Most people want a peaceful trip, but small habits can quickly turn a flight into a nightmare for everyone nearby. Looking back at my years in the sky, here are the main things I wish passengers would stop doing on flights. Depending on the aircraft layout, economy passengers often walked through business class during boarding. I frequently caught people grabbing business-class pillows, premium headphones, or plush blankets on their way back to their seats. Others tried to pack away cabin blankets and safety cards and even pull life vests from under their seats as souvenirs. My crew had to count all those items. Missing life vests meant delaying the flight to replace them, and missing blankets created real supply headaches for our colleagues on the next leg. After the boarding doors closed, I often saw passengers spot an empty business-class seat and try to sneak into it. This almost always happened on long overnight flights when the cabin lights went dim, and people thought we wouldn't notice.

items.text: How Ukraine is taking down Putin’s deadly new drones
items.article: The air defence battle for supremacy over both Russian and Ukrainian cities is becoming a more critical part of the conflict Russia’s latest jet-powered attack drones are forcing Ukraine into a lethal arms race against the clock. A new generation of Russian Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones – which are quicker, more sophisticated and harder for Kyiv’s air defences to intercept – have been hammering its cities. Kyiv is now scrambling to develop defences that can catch them before they reach their targets, with Ukrainian companies developing a new generation of high-speed interceptors designed specifically to hunt them down. It is a game of cat and mouse with deadly consequences . Ukrainian drone maker Wild Hornets says its new Sting S interceptor has destroyed several Geran-5 drones during combat testing, along with roughly a dozen of the slower Geran-4s. It said the interceptions took place over recent weeks and that it plans to begin mass production once all of its testing is complete. The Sting S is one of several interceptor systems that Ukrainian forces are combat-testing in real time in the skies over Ukraine, including the WIV SPYS , developed alongside Germany, and the Zorelit v5 and Zirka, designed to automatically detect and destroy incoming attack drones. The race to develop interceptor systems is a striking new reality of the war: Every time Russia updates its attack drones, Ukraine has to ramp up the weapons used to destroy them, sometimes in a matter of months.
